title: Every variable in all three tests is a function of the same task string, so semantic clustering alone reproduces the paper's entire empirical pattern; no placebo has the right null
location: 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.1 (ll. 38-79), Sec 7.2, Sec 7.3; C_sample_construction.tex ll. 32, 55-60; H_external_validation.tex ll. 419-426
claim: The adjacency variable and the outcome are both produced by running a semantic-similarity operation over the same O*NET task text. (i) The ordering is GPT-5-mini's answer to "Provide the typical sequential order in which these tasks are performed" (E_gpt_prompts.tex Prompt #1), given nothing but the task strings; an LLM handed 20 strings and asked to order them will place textually/topically similar strings adjacently. (ii) is_ai_t is 1 iff Anthropic's pipeline mapped at least one non-filtered Claude conversation to that task string, i.e. iff the string is semantically close to what people bring to Claude; the Eloundou E1/E2 labels are likewise a function of the string. Therefore "AI-executed tasks are adjacent" follows from "topically similar tasks are adjacent" plus "AI-executability is topically clustered," with zero chaining economics. Every placebo in the paper tests against the null "the ordering carries no information at all": the within-occupation position permutation (Sec 7.1, ll. 38-40; Fig. 5 notes ll. 66-68), the within-major-group reassignment, the 1,000 reshuffles behind Fig. 8, and the frequency-cut nulls in G_frequency_robustness.tex l. 81. The paper says as much: "Were the GPT-generated workflow sequences arbitrary... the observed average AI chain length would be a typical draw from the corresponding placebo distribution" (l. 76). That is a straw-man null. No exercise anywhere compares the observed statistics to what a purely topical (non-causal, non-precedence) ordering of the same tasks would produce. Appendix H's summary claims to have answered this: "An instrument that merely clustered semantically similar items would have no reason to place seven in ten consecutive step pairs in the practitioners' direction" (H l. 421). That establishes only that GPT recovers real precedence in the APQC/4TU corpora; it does not establish that the excess chain-clustering in O*NET is driven by the precedence component rather than the topical component of the same ordering. Worse, the PCF re-test (H Sec H.4) transfers labels to PCF steps by nearest-neighbour cosine similarity in all-mpnet-base-v2 space, so the confound is reproduced there rather than removed, and Prediction #3 is not attempted there at all (H: "We do not attempt a counterpart of the neighbor-execution regression").
why_it_matters: This is a single alternative explanation that generates all three headline results simultaneously and requires no economics: no verification fixed cost, no chaining, no firm optimization. If it is right, Sections 7.1-7.3 document that O*NET task statements about writing/analysis/documentation cluster in a GPT-produced list and that Claude is used for writing/analysis/documentation. The paper's entire empirical contribution, and the intro's claim of "new empirical evidence that speaks directly to the core mechanisms emphasized by the model" (1_introduction.tex l. 113), reduces to a text-similarity artifact.
already_addressed: Partially and inadequately. Appendix F varies the prompt (all 11 prompts are LLM orderings of the same strings, so all share the confound; Kendall tau across prompts is 0.6, and H reports the prompts agree with each other at tau 0.79 but with APQC at only 0.53, which is direct evidence that most of what the instrument produces is self-consistent topical structure rather than order). Appendix G prunes infrequent tasks, which does not touch the confound. Appendix H validates that the ordering procedure recovers real precedence on external corpora, and this is genuinely valuable, but validating that the ordering contains SOME precedence signal is not the same as showing that the O*NET results are driven by that signal rather than by the topical signal it also contains. The paper never states the confound in the form given here.
fix: Run a topic-preserving placebo. Embed each occupation's task statements (any sentence encoder), and construct an alternative ordering that is pure topical adjacency with no precedence content: e.g. a greedy nearest-neighbour Hamiltonian path over the embedding graph, or a single-linkage dendrogram leaf order, or a spectral seriation of the cosine-similarity matrix. Recompute (a) mean AI chain length, (b) the EFI regression coefficient beta_2, and (c) the neighbour AMEs on these topical orderings. If the topical ordering delivers chain lengths near 1.45, beta_2 near -0.3, and neighbour AMEs near 0.05, the paper has no result. Additionally, in the Prediction #3 logit, control directly for the cosine similarity between the focal task and each neighbour, so the neighbour coefficients are identified off adjacency conditional on textual similarity; and report the neighbour AME on the subsample of adjacent pairs with LOW textual similarity, which is where genuine precedence-driven chaining should show up most cleanly.

title: Prediction #2's negative EFI coefficient is algebraically forced: EFI conditions on the count of AI-able steps but not on workflow length, and no arrangement placebo is ever run
location: 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.2, eq (2) and ll. 99, 106-115; Table tables/fragmentation_index_regression_exposure.tex; G_frequency_robustness.tex Sec G.3; F_prompt_robustness.tex Sec F.3
claim: Write n for the occupation's task count, k for the number of E1|E2-exposed tasks, b for the number of maximal contiguous runs of exposed tasks. The stated definition ("the ratio of the number of potential tasks... to the total number of steps") gives exactly EFI = (n - k + b)/n = 1 - (k - b)/n. The dependent variable is A/n where A is the number of AI-executed tasks. The regression controls for k ("num_ai_able_steps_o, the number of AI-exposed (E1- or E2-labeled) steps") and for the E1 exposure SHARE, but not for n. The paper's own justification is therefore backwards: "conditioning on that count ensures beta_2 is identified from how the AI-able steps are arranged rather than from how many of them there are" (l. 99). Conditioning on k while leaving n free does the opposite: with k held fixed, EFI = 1 - (k-b)/n is mechanically increasing in n, while the outcome A/n is mechanically decreasing in n whenever A is less than proportional to n (which it must be, since conditional on k the exposure share k/n is falling in n). A negative beta_2 is what this algebra produces before any economics. Two further mechanical channels compound it: (a) under a random arrangement of the same k labels, E[b] = k(n-k+1)/n, so E[EFI] = 1 - k(k-1)/n^2 is a deterministic function of (k,n) alone, i.e. most of the cross-occupation variance in EFI is not arrangement at all; (b) the exposure regressor is the E1 share (Table notes: "'AI Exposure' denotes the share of AI-exposed (E1) steps") while EFI is built from E1|E2 ("We count as AI-exposed both E1- and E2-exposed tasks... 44% of the tasks"), so the E1|E2 exposure share is nowhere controlled and EFI is partly a proxy for it. Note also that the estimated |beta_2| (0.26-0.38) EXCEEDS the exposure coefficient (0.24, 0.11, 0.09) in every column: the paper is asserting that how AI-able steps are arranged matters more for realized AI use than whether they are AI-able at all. That is not a credible economic magnitude; it is the signature of a mechanical relationship. Critically, the paper runs 1,000-draw reshuffle placebos for Prediction #1 (Fig. 5) and Prediction #3 (Fig. 8), and G re-runs both placebos across every frequency cut, but it never once runs a position-reshuffle placebo for equation (2). Appendix F only re-runs it across prompts; Appendix G only re-runs it across frequency cuts.
why_it_matters: Prediction #2 is the paper's flagship empirical claim, the one promoted to the abstract and to 1_introduction.tex ll. 97 and 123 ("occupations whose AI-exposed steps are more dispersed across the production workflow exhibit a substantially lower share of their steps executed by AI"). It is also the only test that maps to a named proposition. If beta_2 < 0 is reproduced by randomly rearranging the same exposure labels, the result is a restatement of the definition of EFI, and Section 7.2 and the intro claim collapse. This is also the most predictable referee request in the paper, since the authors already run exactly this placebo twice elsewhere.
already_addressed: No. Grepping G_frequency_robustness.tex and F_prompt_robustness.tex confirms the reshuffle placebo is applied to chain length (G l. 81, Fig. G.2) and to the neighbour AMEs (G l. 178, Fig. G.5) but never to equation (2); F Sec F.3 varies only the prompt. The paper does acknowledge mechanicalness for EFI Definition 2 (D_tables_and_robustness.tex: "the execution-based EFI measure is mechanically related to the share of tasks executed by AI") but explicitly presents Definition 1 as the clean, ex-ante measure. Workflow length n is never controlled in eq (2); by contrast the Prediction #3 logit does control for it ("we also control for... number of steps in the occupation it appears in", l. 187), which makes the omission in eq (2) look like an oversight rather than a choice.
fix: Three things, all cheap. (1) Add n (and n^2, or the E1|E2 exposure share) to eq (2) and report how beta_2 moves; better, replace EFI by a residualized arrangement measure such as b - E[b | k, n] (excess number of runs relative to the random-arrangement benchmark), which is orthogonal to (k, n) by construction. (2) Run the position-reshuffle placebo on eq (2) itself: 1,000 within-occupation permutations, recompute EFI, re-estimate, and plot the observed beta_2 against the null distribution exactly as in Figures 5 and 8. Report the percentile. (3) Report beta_2 in levels as well as standardized units, and state the clustering level for the standard errors, which the table notes never do (872 occupations, 872 observations, "Clustered standard errors" clustered on what?).

title: Prediction #3 regresses one realized chain membership on another: the coefficient is the definition of a chain, not a behavioural response, and the reported AME is the wrong statistic
claim: In equation (3) both is_ai_t and prev_is_ai_t / next_is_ai_t are outcomes of the same firm cost-minimization; the model contains no response function of step t to its neighbours' realized status. Two adjacent steps are in the same chain if and only if each is the other's AI neighbour, so on the subsample where chaining actually occurs the regression estimates Definition 4, not behaviour. This is the textbook simultaneity/reflection problem (Manski 1993) in its starkest form: endogenous, contextual and correlated effects are all loaded onto beta_2 and beta_3, and no fixed effect can separate them. DWA fixed effects (column 4) address only the correlated-effects channel operating through task type, and only its DWA mean; SOC major/minor FE are at the 2- and 3-digit level. There is NO occupation fixed effect and no control for the occupation's own AI-execution share. That omission is decisive: Computer Programmers has two thirds of its tasks AI-executed and Electronic Equipment Installers has none (C_sample_construction.tex Figures C.3, C.5), so within a high-intensity occupation every task has high is_ai AND high neighbour is_ai purely by composition, with no adjacency content whatsoever. The neighbours' AI EXPOSURE is also never controlled, only the focal task's own ("we also control for the step t's AI exposure status", l. 187), so the neighbour-execution dummy proxies for the focal task's own residual latent AI-ability through topical similarity. Finally, the paper reports the wrong number as its result. It knows the placebo distributions are not centred at zero ("across all neighbors within each specification, the randomized distributions are centered at similar means", l. 272) but never reports where they are centred, and the headline claim is stated in raw AMEs (0.05, 0.04 under DWA FE). Since the within-occupation reshuffle preserves occupation AI intensity, the null mean IS the composition effect, and the only interpretable estimand is the gap between the observed AME and that null mean. That gap appears nowhere in the paper; the reader is shown only that the red line "lie[s] to the right of the randomized distributions" (l. 275).
why_it_matters: Prediction #3 is the one test the paper presents as a within-step comparison ("when the same step appears in two occupations..."), and it is the basis for the conclusion's claim that neighbouring steps make a task "significantly more likely to be executed by AI" (8_conclusion.tex l. 14). As specified it identifies neither a neighbour effect nor anything the model predicts, and its reported magnitude is inflated by an occupation-composition component of unreported size. It is also not an independent test: a positive lag-1 autocorrelation of is_ai within an occupation is arithmetically the same fact as a mean run length above 1, so Prediction #3 as run is Prediction #1 re-estimated with covariates, not a second piece of evidence.
already_addressed: Partially. The reshuffle placebos in Figure 8 and G Fig. G.5 do handle the "could this arise by chance under random ordering" question, and D_tables_and_robustness.tex Sec D.3 tightens task similarity via a GPT filter and re-runs on is_automated. But none of these touches simultaneity, none adds an occupation fixed effect or an occupation AI-intensity control, none controls neighbours' exposure, and the excess-over-null magnitude is never reported. The GPT-similarity filter makes the tasks more comparable, which is the correlated-effects channel again, not the endogenous-effects one.
fix: Estimate the model's actual reduced form instead: regress is_ai_t on the neighbours' AI EXPOSURE (prev_exposed, next_exposed, prev2_exposed, next2_exposed), controlling for the focal task's own exposure and with DWA FE. Neighbour difficulty d_i is the exogenous primitive in the model; neighbour execution is not. That specification is neither mechanical nor reflective, and it is the one the theory delivers. Then (a) add occupation fixed effects, or at minimum the leave-one-out occupation AI-execution share, to every column and show what survives; (b) report, for each specification, the observed AME, the reshuffle-null mean, and their difference with a permutation p-value, and make the DIFFERENCE the headline number in the text and abstract; (c) state explicitly that the estimand is a conditional association, not a neighbour effect, or drop the language of "effect" from the table titles.

title: The tested predictions are not propositions of the model, and the paper's own worked example implies Prediction #2 has no sign
claim: Proposition 2 states that the fragmentation index is within a constant factor of the optimal COST: (1/8)OPT <= FI <= (5/4)OPT. It says nothing about the SHARE of steps executed by AI, which is the dependent variable of equation (2). The paper's own leading example says the opposite of what it tests: after Example 4 (clustered AI-able steps), 4_implications.tex l. 186 reads "The same two steps are executed by AI either way, since an isolated easy step is already worth augmenting on its own; what the arrangement changes is what that AI execution costs." In the paper's flagship illustration of the fragmentation mechanism, moving from dispersed to clustered leaves the AI-executed SET unchanged, i.e. beta_2 = 0. The empirical prediction is then rescued in a single unformalized sentence: "Where an isolated exposed step is not worth augmenting on its own, a case the model equally permits, dispersion suppresses AI execution outright rather than merely making it dearer, and it is that margin the AI-execution shares of Section 7 pick up" (l. 187). "A case the model equally permits" is not a prediction; it is the admission that the model permits both signs and that which one obtains depends on unobserved (m_i, a_i, alpha). The same gap applies to the other two tests: no proposition states that AI-executed steps form runs longer than random (Prediction #1), and no proposition states that a step's neighbours' realized status raises its own execution probability (Prediction #3). The Section 7 text derives all three from "Examples 3 and 4" and from Definition 4, i.e. from a definition and two numerical illustrations. On top of this, Prediction #1 as tested is not even about the model's chain object: the model requires every non-terminal step of a chain to be AUTOMATED, and the paper discards that requirement because the data contradicts it ("We therefore do not distinguish the two labels in what follows and treat both as indicating AI execution", l. 28; App C.1). A run of AI-executed steps in which none is automated is not an AI chain in the model's sense and involves no amortized verification.
why_it_matters: ReStud will judge this paper on its theory. A theory paper whose empirical section tests three informal intuitions rather than any stated result, and one of whose tests has an ambiguous sign in the model's own worked example, cannot claim its evidence supports the model. Worse, since the model permits beta_2 >= 0, a negative estimate is not a rejection of anything, which strips the exercise of falsification content and leaves it, together with Finding 2 (the mechanical channel), with no informational value at all.
already_addressed: No. Section 7 asserts the sign ("The model predicts... beta_2 < 0", l. 101) with the Examples as the only support, and never flags that the sign is conditional on a parameter region. Appendix A proves Proposition 2 in cost terms. Nothing in D, F, G or H addresses the theory-to-prediction mapping. Section 7 does not derive equation (3) from the model at all.
fix: State and prove a proposition with the AI-execution SHARE, not cost, on the left-hand side: give sufficient conditions on (m_i, a_i, d_i, alpha) under which a mean-preserving clustering of AI-able steps weakly raises the number of AI-executed steps, and state the region where it does not. If a clean condition is unavailable, simulate the short-run cost-minimization over the empirically relevant parameter space, regress the simulated AI-execution share on the simulated EFI with the same controls as equation (2), and report the sign and magnitude of the model-implied beta_2 as the benchmark against which the estimate is read. Do the analogous exercise to generate the model-implied mean chain length and the model-implied neighbour AME, so that all three tests have quantitative predictions rather than sign predictions. Separately, either restrict Prediction #1 to runs containing at least one automated step, or state plainly that the tested object is looser than the model's chain.

title: The economic magnitude of the paper's central mechanism is never reported, and mean chain length 1.45 suggests it is rare
claim: The paper's engine is that verification is a fixed cost of a chain rather than a marginal cost per step, which pays off only when a chain has length >= 2 (a length-1 chain is ordinary augmentation with its own verification, and needs none of the theory). The only magnitude reported is "The observed mean AI chain length is 1.45" (l. 44), and the comparison is stated qualitatively: "noticeably larger than in both placebo distributions" (l. 72). The main text never reports the placebo null mean, its standard deviation, a z-statistic or a p-value (the 100th-percentile figure appears only in G_frequency_robustness.tex, and the null mean for the O*NET sample appears nowhere; the analogous PCF numbers, null 1.07 vs observed 1.14, are given in H l. 368, so the authors clearly know how to report them). More importantly, the paper never reports the distribution of chain lengths, the number of chains of length >= 2, or the share of AI-executed steps that sit in a run of length >= 2. With a mean of 1.45 the modal chain is a singleton, and the fraction of AI-executed steps that participate in the mechanism the paper is built on is plausibly around half or less. The paper itself concedes the implication when interpreting Prediction #3: "This aligns with the relatively short average AI chain length observed in the data (mean length 1.45), implying that tasks two positions away rarely fall in the same chain as the focal task" (l. 281). The Prediction #3 table likewise reports no economic benchmark, and the paper says so: "Because we do not have a benchmark for what constitutes a large versus small effect in our context, interpreting the magnitudes in a vacuum is difficult" (l. 213).
why_it_matters: Statistical distinguishability from a random-ordering null is not evidence that chaining organizes AI adoption in the economy. If most realized AI use is isolated single-step augmentation, the paper has documented a small, statistically detectable clustering tendency and built a 45-page theory of verification amortization on top of it, while the empirical section provides no evidence on how much of observed AI adoption the mechanism actually accounts for. A ReStud referee reading '1.45' with no null mean beside it will not accept 'noticeably larger' as a result statement.
already_addressed: Partly, and only in the appendices. G_frequency_robustness.tex l. 84 reports the full-sample value sits at the 100th percentile of its null and that chain length falls to 1.24-1.31 under most frequency cuts, and H l. 368 reports the PCF null explicitly and concedes "The economic magnitude of AI chain length is therefore modest." That concession never reaches Section 7 or the abstract. The chain-length distribution and the share of AI steps in runs of length >= 2 are reported nowhere in the paper.
fix: In Section 7.1, report: the full distribution of chain lengths (counts at 1, 2, 3, 4+); the share of AI-executed steps in runs of length >= 2 and the same share for the reshuffle null; the null mean, SD, z and permutation p for the mean-chain-length statistic; and the same figures restricted to runs containing at least one automated step, which is the model's actual chain. Then state what fraction of realized AI execution the chaining mechanism can be responsible for, and carry that honest number into the abstract and introduction.

title: Standard errors in Prediction #3 are clustered on the wrong dimension: each task enters as focal once and as a regressor up to four times, within occupation, and occupation dependence is entirely unclustered
location: 7_empirics.tex Table 4 notes (l. 200 ff.: "Standard errors are bootstrapped using B=200 replications and clustered at the DWA level"); tables/noTasksWithRepetitiveDWAs/allTasks_ai.tex
claim: Equation (3) has a spatial-lag structure along the occupation's sequence: task t's outcome is task (t+1)'s prev_is_ai regressor and task (t-1)'s next_is_ai regressor. The resulting error dependence runs along the OCCUPATION dimension. Clustering is at the DWA level, and the sample is built precisely so that tasks in the same occupation belong to different DWAs ("we drop tasks that are mapped to multiple DWAs. We further restrict attention to DWAs that contain tasks appearing in more than one occupation"). So the within-occupation dependence induced by the overlapping regressors is not absorbed by DWA clustering at all, and the reported standard errors are understated by an unknown factor. The bootstrap is a DWA cluster bootstrap and inherits the same problem. Separately, the same table has an unexplained sample discontinuity: column (5) is described in the text as the baseline plus the same-DWA-count control ("Columns (5)-(6) repeat the exercise controlling for the number of same-DWA tasks in the focal task's occupation") but is estimated on N = 4,096 rather than 10,708, with pseudo-R^2 collapsing from 0.112 to 0.030; nothing in the text or notes accounts for the 62% sample loss in a column with no fixed effects.
why_it_matters: The surviving result under the most demanding specification is an AME of 0.05 with a standard error of 0.02 (column 4). It is significant at 5%, not 1%, and there is no margin for an understated standard error. If two-way (occupation, DWA) clustering widens it by even a modest factor, the one specification that holds task type fixed loses conventional significance and Prediction #3 has no surviving estimate.
already_addressed: No. The clustering level is stated but never justified, and no alternative clustering is reported anywhere in the main text, D, F, G or H. G l. 16 notes that the frequency-cut tables use analytic robust SEs clustered at the DWA level instead of the bootstrap, which is the same dimension. The reshuffle placebo in Figure 8 is a valid inference procedure and does not depend on the clustering choice, which is a further reason to make the placebo gap the headline statistic rather than the table's stars.
fix: Report two-way clustering on (occupation, DWA) for every column of Table 4 and the corresponding appendix tables; if the number of occupations is too small in the DWA-FE sample, report an occupation-block bootstrap instead. Explain the column (5) sample restriction, or estimate it on the full 10,708.

title: The outcome variable is Claude-only consumer usage with content-correlated false negatives coded as 'manual', and the appendix's claim that this only costs power is wrong
claim: is_ai is constructed as follows: of ~18,000 O*NET tasks, 3,364 are linked to Claude conversations, 1,017 of those have 100% of conversations filtered, and "we treat tasks that do not appear in the Anthropic dataset, as well as those with 100% filtered conversations, as manual tasks" (l. 32). So roughly 87% of the outcome's zeros are non-observations, and the 1,017 fully-filtered tasks are known false negatives: the appendix concedes "we know that all of them were executed in some way using Claude" (l. 143). The Filtered category is defined by non-classifiability and privacy sensitivity, which is a function of task CONTENT, i.e. of exactly the dimension along which the GPT ordering places tasks. The appendix then argues "excluding them limits our statistical power" (l. 144) and that tool specialization "would primarily reduce our statistical power rather than generate artificial patterns" (l. 151). That is not right for a binary outcome whose false negatives are content-correlated: content-correlated dropouts inside a chain break runs and depress mean chain length (attenuating Prediction #1), and inside eq (2) they make the dependent variable partly a measure of Anthropic's task-mapping COVERAGE for that occupation rather than of realized AI execution, which biases beta_1 and beta_2 in directions the paper has not signed. Separately, the unit mismatch is never confronted: the model's decision-maker is a firm choosing an AI strategy for a workflow to minimize cost, whereas the Anthropic Economic Index records individual Claude.ai conversations classified by topic. Nobody in the data is executing an occupation's workflow, and no firm's chaining decision is observed. Two adjacent tasks being 'AI-executed' means two different people used Claude for two topically related things, not that one firm ran a chain.
why_it_matters: The confounds in Findings 1-3 all operate through task content. An outcome variable whose measurement error is itself a function of task content is the worst possible companion to those confounds, because it makes the direction of bias unsignable rather than merely conservative. And the unit mismatch means the paper's central object, the firm's chain, is never observed even in principle, which caps how much any of these tests can say about the model.
already_addressed: Partially, in C_sample_construction.tex ll. 141-153. The appendix flags the fully-filtered tasks and the Claude-only coverage and argues both are conservative, but the argument is asserted rather than demonstrated ("We do not have a reason to believe this is the case", l. 150 footnote) and the classical-measurement-error intuition invoked does not apply. The unit mismatch between a firm cost-minimization problem and consumer conversation logs is never raised anywhere in the paper.
fix: (1) Bound the filtering problem: re-run all three tests coding the 1,017 fully-filtered tasks as AI-executed, and again dropping them, and report the range. (2) Show that the fully-filtered tasks are not systematically positioned in the workflow (e.g. compare their mean normalized sequence position and mean exposure share to those of classified tasks). (3) In eq (2), control for the occupation's Anthropic coverage rate (share of its tasks appearing in the Anthropic mapping at all) so that beta_1 and beta_2 are not identified off coverage. (4) State plainly in Section 7 that the data records individual AI use by topic and not firm workflow decisions, and say what that limits.
